::: {.callout-note}
**Inference lab** using the five-step template:
Hypothesis → Visualise → Assumptions → Conduct → Conclude.
:::

## Learning objectives

- Define MCAR, MAR, and MNAR and give an example of each.
- Simulate the three mechanisms and measure the bias in a
  complete-case analysis.
- Decide when a missingness assumption is defensible from the data
  alone and when it is not.

## Prerequisites

Course 2 regression basics.

## Background

The language of missingness is Rubin's taxonomy. MCAR (missing
completely at random) means the probability of being missing does
not depend on anything — observed or unobserved. MAR (missing at
random) means the probability depends only on observed variables.
MNAR (missing not at random) means the probability depends on the
missing value itself, even after conditioning on everything
observed. Each is a property of the process, not the data, and you
can rarely decide between MAR and MNAR from the data alone.

Complete-case analysis drops rows with missing values. For the unadjusted
marginal mean in this example, MCAR gives unbiased estimation in repeated
sampling. Under MAR, validity depends on the estimand and model: a correctly
specified outcome regression can remain valid when missingness depends only
on observed predictors. MNAR requires additional identifying assumptions and sensitivity analysis.
Multiple imputation under MAR also needs a correctly specified imputation
model compatible with the analysis; it does not resolve MNAR automatically.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Auxiliary variables — things that correlate with both the outcome
and the missingness but are not in the analysis model — are the
currency of MAR. If you have them, put them in the imputation
model. If you do not, your MAR claim is on thinner ice than it
appears.
:::

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(42)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## 1. Hypothesis

We estimate the mean of Y from each of three datasets with the same
true mean, where Y has been made missing by MCAR, MAR, and MNAR
processes.

## 2. Visualise

```{r}
n  <- 1000
df <- tibble(
  x = rnorm(n, 50, 10),
  y = 2 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(n, 0, 5)
)

mcar <- df |> mutate(y_obs = if_else(runif(n) < 0.30, NA_real_, y),
                     mech  = "MCAR")
mar  <- df |> mutate(p = plogis(-2 + 0.05 * (x - 50)),
                     y_obs = if_else(runif(n) < p, NA_real_, y),
                     mech  = "MAR")
mnar <- df |> mutate(p = plogis(-2 + 0.05 * (y - mean(y))),
                     y_obs = if_else(runif(n) < p, NA_real_, y),
                     mech  = "MNAR")

all <- bind_rows(
  mcar |> select(mech, x, y, y_obs),
  mar  |> select(mech, x, y, y_obs),
  mnar |> select(mech, x, y, y_obs)
)

all |>
  mutate(missing = is.na(y_obs)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = missing)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ mech) +
  labs(colour = "Y missing?")
```

## 3. Assumptions

Complete-case analysis is the bluntest possible method. It is
justified if missingness is MCAR. We will compute the mean of Y on
observed rows for each mechanism and compare with the true mean.

## 4. Conduct

```{r}
results <- all |>
  group_by(mech) |>
  summarise(
    truth = mean(y),
    cc    = mean(y_obs, na.rm = TRUE),
    bias  = cc - truth,
    pct_missing = mean(is.na(y_obs)) * 100
  )
results
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
results |>
  ggplot(aes(mech, bias)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.7, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Bias of complete-case mean")
```

## 5. Concluding statement

> In this single simulation, complete-case minus full-data mean was
> `r round(results$bias[results$mech == "MCAR"], 2)` under MCAR,
> `r round(results$bias[results$mech == "MAR"], 2)` under MAR, and
> `r round(results$bias[results$mech == "MNAR"], 2)` under MNAR.
> These are observed differences in one sample, not repeated-simulation
> estimates of bias. The missingness fractions also differ by mechanism.

To estimate bias, repeat the simulation and average the estimation error
against the known population mean. The companion app provides repeated draws.

::: {.notes}
Students often ask how to test for MCAR. Little's test exists but
can only reject MCAR; it cannot prove it. The assumption ultimately
rests on argument, not on a *p*-value.
:::

## Common pitfalls

- Using Little's test as evidence *for* MCAR.
- Imputing with a model that omits the analysis outcome.
- Reporting a sample size inflated by a complete-case filter that
  hides 40% dropout.
- Using "the missingness was not significantly related to X" as
  proof of MAR.

## Further reading

- Little RJA, Rubin DB. *Statistical Analysis with Missing Data*.
- van Buuren S (2018), *Flexible Imputation of Missing Data*.
- Sterne JA et al. (2009), *Multiple imputation for missing data
  in epidemiological and clinical research*.
